title: Given distinct candidates and a target, return all unique combinations that sum to target. Each candidate may be used an unlimited number of times.
shortTitle: Combination Sum — reusable candidates, keep index to dedup

s1_definition.profdef: Depth-first backtracking that, at each step, either reuses the current candidate (recurse with the same index, allowing repeats) or advances to the next candidate. Passing the current index (not index+1) when reusing permits unlimited repetition while the non-decreasing index order prevents permutations of the same combination. A branch is recorded when the remaining target hits zero and pruned when it goes negative.
s1_definition.analogy: A customer at National Bank of India wants to reach an exact savings target using fixed-denomination recurring deposits, and the same denomination can be used many times. You try adding a denomination, keep trying the same one as long as the target is not exceeded, and whenever you hit the target exactly you record that plan.
s1_definition.oneliner: Recurse with the same index to allow reuse; stop at zero, prune below zero, advance index to avoid reordered duplicates.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Depth-first backtracking that, at each step, either reuses the current candidate (recurse with the same index, allowing repeats) or advances to the next candidate. Passing the current index (not index+1) when reusing permits unlimited repetition while the non-decreasing index order prevents permutations of the same combination. A branch is recorded when the remaining target hits zero and pruned when it goes negative.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A customer at National Bank of India wants to reach an exact savings target using fixed-denomination recurring deposits, and the same denomination can be used many times. You try adding a denomination, keep trying the same one as long as the target is not exceeded, and whenever you hit the target exactly you record that plan.

**One line to remember:** Recurse with the same index to allow reuse; stop at zero, prune below zero, advance index to avoid reordered duplicates.

sections.s2_technical:
Carry a start index, the remaining target, and the current path. If remaining is zero, record a copy; if negative, return. Otherwise loop from start, subtract the candidate, recurse with the same index to allow reuse, then backtrack. For example: `path.add(cand[i]); backtrack(i, remain - cand[i]); path.remove(last);`.

Passing `i` rather than `i+1` is what permits the same candidate to repeat; keeping the loop starting at `start` prevents going backward, which is what stops reordered duplicates like [2,3] and [3,2].

Sorting candidates lets you break early when a candidate exceeds the remaining target. The time is exponential in the worst case, bounded by the number of combinations times their length. A senior nuance is that pruning with a sorted array (`if (cand[i] > remain) break;`) dramatically cuts the search on realistic inputs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a customer wants to reach an exact goal amount using recurring deposit slabs of fixed denominations, reusing any slab as many times as needed. The advisor must list every plan that hits the goal. This is exactly how Combination Sum works.

Problem 2 — Two plans with the same slabs in a different order are the same plan and must appear once. This is exactly why the start index never goes backward.

The mini-project builds a `DepositPlanFinder`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input slabs two, three, five target eight.

Step 1: Choosing two repeatedly builds [2,2,2,2] which sums to eight and is recorded.

Step 2: The path [2,3,3] sums to eight and is recorded, reached by reusing three after a two.

Step 3: The path [3,5] sums to eight and is recorded.

Step 4: Branches that overshoot eight are pruned by the sorted break, and the index never going backward keeps each plan in non-decreasing order.

```text
2026-10-27T00:05:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Recurring Deposit Plan Finder (Combination Sum)
2026-10-27T00:05:00Z [INFO] Found 3 deposit plans for target 8
2026-10-27T00:05:00Z [INFO] Plan: [2, 2, 2, 2]
2026-10-27T00:05:00Z [INFO] Plan: [2, 3, 3]
2026-10-27T00:05:00Z [INFO] Plan: [3, 5]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  sort [2,3,5], target=8
    reuse same index i → repeats allowed
      [2,2,2,2]=8   [2,3,3]=8   [3,5]=8
    remain<0 → prune ; cand[i]>remain → break
  plans = 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Combination Sum asks for every combination of candidates that sums to a target, where each candidate can be used any number of times. I solve it with backtracking that carries a start index and the remaining target. When the remaining target reaches zero I record the current path, and if it ever goes negative I abandon the branch. The crucial detail is that when I recurse after choosing a candidate I pass the same index rather than the next one, which is what allows a candidate to be reused as many times as needed.

Keeping the loop anchored at the start index, so it never goes backward, is what guarantees each combination appears in non-decreasing order and therefore only once, rather than as several reordered duplicates. Sorting the candidates lets me break out of the loop as soon as a candidate exceeds the remaining target, which prunes the search sharply.

In my project at National Bank of India, an advisor tool listed every recurring-deposit plan built from fixed denomination slabs that reached a customer's exact savings goal, with slabs reusable without limit. This backtracking produced all valid plans, and the sorted-break pruning kept it responsive even for larger goals.
